title: Characteristics of an Integrated Micro Packed Bed Reactor-Heat Exchanger for methanol synthesis from syngas
abstract: The main characteristics of a multi-slit Integrated Micro Packed Bed Reactor-Heat Exchanger (IMPBRHE) for compact synthesis of methanol from syngas over a Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst under industrial operating conditions (80bar and 523K) were investigated. The reaction experiments show that near equilibrium conversion per pass is achievable at low contact times (about 470ms g/ml). The experiments show superior heat removal capability from the catalytic slits through isothermal conditions. Pressure drop measurements in agreement with calculation by Ergun equation indicate an isobaric reaction media in the slits. The IMPBRHE shows promising features for further research on process intensification and miniaturization.
paragraphs: The proven natural gas reserves in the world exceed 170TCM (trillion cubic meter), of which about one-third can be classified as stranded gas. A considerable amount of stranded gas reserves are located off shore with low economic incentive to be produced, transported and sold. Considering the growing demand in the fuel and chemicals market, finding economic and environmentally sustainable solutions for utilization of more of the proven reserves is imperative.

Among different approaches to remote off shore natural gas monetization, on-site conversion into readily transportable fuels such as diesel, naphtha, methanol and DME is of great interest. Existing technologies for natural gas conversion benefit from economy of scale. The preferred technology for large-scale conversion also exhibits features which may be unfavourable or unsafe in floating installations, such as slurry columns, cryogenic oxygen production units and large burners. An effective down-scale approach with highly efficient unit operations is hence needed

Limitations in space and weight, as well as demanding conditions on site, call for highly integrated, compact, light-weight weight and safe technology. Microchannel reactors have the potential to meet such requirements, and hence transform the economics of these processes. These reactors consist of parallel arrays of channels with critical dimensions typically in the range of 0.25–2mm. Small channel dimensions provide high surface-to-volume ratios, greatly enhancing both heat and mass transfer. The high rates of heat and mass transfer allow utilization of the most active catalysts with higher reaction rates than conventional reactors. The result could be increased product yields, improved energy efficiency, smaller reactor footprint, and reduced capital costs. Microreaction technology could be a particularly interesting choice for the Fischer–Tropsch, methanol and DME syntheses, where highly exothermic and sometimes complex reaction systems are linked to the selectivity and/or reactor performance.

Velocys, a spin-off of the Battelle Memorial Institute, owns many patents on application of Micro Process Technology in natural gas conversion, including synthesis gas, methanol and Fischer–Tropsch technologies. Daly and Tonkovich studied their so-called “isopotential” microchannel reactor, where narrow channels and highly active catalyst formulations for methanol synthesis were applied. They showed that the microchannel reactor is isothermal and that it could outperform a tubular fixed-bed reactor at low contact times. Based on this, they later suggested a floating, production, storage and offloading (FPSO) multiple microchannel concept for 1000 TPD (tons per day) methanol plant with a carbon efficiency of around 56%.

Performance of monolithic catalysts made of cordierite and γ-Al2O3 for the Fischer–Tropsch (FT) synthesis was also investigated by Schanke et al. and Hilmen et al. in the late 1990s. Myrstad et al. recently studied Fischer–Tropsch synthesis in a microstructured reactor synthesis. They demonstrated the microstructured reactor's capability to operate with highly active, undiluted catalysts at severe conditions without causing temperature runaways and thus avoiding enhanced deactivation of the catalyst.

Heatric, claiming the Printed Circuit Heat Exchangers (PCHE) technology, has applied its core competence to develop technologies for off shore gas conversion including FT and methanol synthesis. They suggest that in selecting between a FT or methanol compact plant, the latter would be the choice. FT catalyst with its complex operating environment has a lower specific productivity than a methanol catalyst, which inevitably results in a larger reactor. The unique potential of the methanol synthesis lies in its exothermicity and limitation by thermodynamic equilibrium, that makes it possible to increase the productivity and decrease the size by superior thermal management. For a feed gas composed of up to 25% vol. CO2, a carbon efficiency of about 65% is claimed.

Ajmera et al. applied microfabricated silicon cross flow reactor for catalyst testing and kinetic analysis. The outcome of their reactor characteristics study was that the reaction medium is isobaric and that the pressure drop in their cross flow microchannel reactor is much lower than in a conventional fixed-bed configuration. They demonstrated absence of transport limitations and well distributed flow in the multichannel system. Using CO oxidation as model reaction, they advocated application of such devices for kinetic analysis. In an earlier work, they also showed application of this configuration for safe synthesis of hazardous compounds such as phosgene.

Since fixed-bed technology is well known, it would be very beneficial if one could apply some of the existing knowledge and technology into micro scale. While wall coated microchannels could suffer from lower productivity per unit reactor volume, the micro packed bed reactors could potentially load more catalyst to give higher productivities, provided that heat and mass transfer limitations are negligible. Catalyst pellets in industrial applications are in comparison rather large (between 2 and 6mm), and some exhibit a so-called eggshell distribution of the active material if the core of the pellet is not efficiently utilized due to mass transfer limitations. Another advantage of micro packed reactors could therefore be the applicability of the most active existing catalysts in a particle size range of 500μm or less. Using existing or well explored catalyst systems may furthermore enable the application of kinetic data readily available in the literature in the performance assessment of the reactor. Moreover, there is no extra coating development necessary. Ensuring even distribution of such small particles in all of the parallel channels, as well as minimizing the pressure drop has, however, been regarded as serious challenges to microchannel reactor technology. The former affects the flow pattern and hence the residence time distribution, and the latter the operating costs. The possibility of easy catalyst replacement is a final positive aspect of micro packed bed reactors, in laboratory research as well as industrial applications.

The methanol synthesis is a mature and well-developed process and many large industrial plants are under operation. Companies such as Haldor Topsøe, Lurgi, Davy Process Technology and Mitsubishi Gas Chemicals are leading in this technology. The methanol formation is based on the following three reactions, of which only two are independent: (1) CO2 +3H2 ↔CH3OH+H2O(ΔH 298 =−49kJ/mol) (2) CO+2H2 ↔CH3OH(ΔH 298 =−91kJ/mol) (3) CO+H2O↔H2 +CO2 (ΔH 298 =41kJ/mol)

CuO/ZnO/oxidic support is the commonly used catalyst systems and the reaction mechanism over this catalyst has been under some debate. Most now seem to agree that methanol mainly forms from CO2 under relevant conditions. To balance the formation (1) and consumption of water (3), the synthesis gas feedstock normally contains CO, CO2 and H2 with the so-called methanol module ((H2-CO)/(CO+CO2)) close to 2.

Due to both the thermodynamic equilibrium and the high exothermicity, the single-pass conversion of CO is relatively low and the maximum CO content in fresh feed gas in large-scale methanol reactors is limited to around 16%. A high recycle flow of unconverted gas is hence necessary to ensure high total conversion in commercial methanol plants. The equilibrium is favoured by high pressure and low temperature, but the choice of conditions has to be compromised against other requirements, such as kinetics (temperature). The formation of methanol causes a 67% decrease in number of moles; hence the reaction is favoured by high pressure. Because of the exothermicity, however, elevated pressure usually results in higher exit temperatures and thus lower equilibrium conversion. High temperatures also lead to deactivation and increased formation of undesired products such as ethanol and methyl formate. The generated heat therefore has to be efficiently dissipated to maintain optimum catalyst lifetime, activity and selectivity.

As part of a large research project entitled “Enabling Production of Remote Gas”, the present work investigates the main characteristics of an Integrated Micro Packed Bed Reactor-Heat Exchanger (IMPBRHE) for synthesis of methanol from synthesis gas. Particular attention is paid to the capability of heat removal and isothermal operation of the IMPBRHE as well as determining the impact of potential drawbacks of micro packed bed reactors such as pressure drop. Design considerations of the IMPBRHE as well as the performance of a Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst for methanol synthesis using the IMPBRHE is presented and discussed.

The IMPBRHE was fabricated by the Institute of Micro Process Engineering (IMVT) at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), formerly Forschungszentrum Karlsruhe, in Germany. The microstructured reactor module is made in stainless steel and designed for up to 100bar pressure. The module consists of eight reaction slits and each reaction slit is sandwiched between two cross flow oil channels for heat transfer. A schematic picture of the reactor module and sketch of the arrangement are shown in Fig. 1a and b, respectively.

The catalyst slits (channels) are made by etching 0.4mm deep hexagonally arranged cylindrical pillar structures in 1mm stainless steel foils. A SEM picture of an etched catalyst slit is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Diffusion bonding of two foils face to face gives a 0.8mm deep pillar structure. The reaction slits (with the integrated pillars) are 60mm in length with cross section of (8.0mm×0.8mm). One of the catalyst foils has a “missing row” of pillars with room for a 0.5mm thermocouple which could be used for temperature measurements inside the middle reaction slit. Three tiny holes along the centreline of the reaction zone on top of the outer surface of the reactor could alternatively be used for (skin) temperature measurements, providing close proximity to the cooling channels and reaction slits (1mm distance to the cooling channels and 2mm to the reaction slits). Two frits (porous metallic plates) were used at the reaction zone inlet and outlet to keep the catalyst particles in place and to improve the flow distribution. For heat exchange, 0.25mm×0.5mm cross flow oil channels with 0.25mm×0.25mm fins between are made in 0.5mm metal foils.

A high temperature oil thermostat (Julabo HT30) was used to maintain the temperature up to 575K at low-pressure levels. The reactor module was insulated properly to minimize heat losses and avoid disturbances in skin temperature measurements.

The Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst was synthesized according to the standard precipitation procedure developed by ICI. BET and ICP-AES measurements were applied to investigate the catalyst surface area and composition, respectively, and the results are shown in Table 1 . The sodium impurity level was found to be within the range proposed by ICI to have negligible effect. Temperature Programmed Reduction (TPR) of the catalyst sample showed that the reduction interval is 456–553K with a peak at 536K, in agreement with similar work. A fraction of sieved catalyst with particle diameter of 50–120μm was loaded into the IMPBRHE slits in dry form. The catalyst was divided into portions. Each portion was placed above the entrance of the slits and would readily enter the slits upon gentle manual vibration. Great care was taken to ensure that approximately equal amounts of catalyst were loaded into each slit. Visual inspection of a glass model of the slit structure filled with two differently coloured particles indicated an even particle distribution along the slit. The pillar structure was found not to cause any difficulties in loading, neither to have influence on the particle distribution inside the slits. A mixture of 3 H2 vol.% in N2 was used to reduce the catalyst by increasing the temperature to 528K over 24h followed by dwelling at this temperature for 6h, before introducing the reaction gas and pressure build – up to 80bar.

Premixed synthesis gas H2/CO/CO2/N2 (65/25/5/5mol%) was used. The synthesis gas was passed through a bed containing lead oxide to remove potential carbonyl type impurities. Possible oxygen and humidity contents were also removed. Digital mass flow controllers (Bronkhorst) were used to adjust the gas flow to the reactors. The feed gas temperature was kept constant and equal to the reaction temperature unless otherwise mentioned. The contact time (τ) is defined as the ratio of catalyst mass/syngas flow rate at STP. The product stream was first cooled to ambient temperature where most of the methanol and water were collected. The liquid phase products were directed to an atmospheric pressure vessel and collected. A cooling bath was then used to collect small amounts of non-condensed products. Pressure drop measurements were made by a smart differential pressure transmitter (APLISENS, APR-2000) with an accuracy of ±0.1mbar. The sensors were located as close as possible to the reactor inlet and outlet in order to provide precise measurements. The feed and product gases were analyzed by GC (Agilent 6890) equipped with a Thermal Conductivity Detector (TCD) in online mode, while the liquid products were analyzed offline using a Flame Ionization Detector (FID) through manual injection, closing the carbon balance within 5% in most experiments.

Conversion data as function of temperature (measured on the reactor skin, middle position) and contact time are shown in Figs. 3 and 4 , respectively. A continuous, slow decrease in the catalyst activity amounting to a decrease in conversion from 37% to 26% at 528K and 80bar was observed during the approximately 300h on stream. The conversion values shown in Figs. 3 and 4 have therefore been compensated for the extent of deactivation at the point of measurement. A linear fit was used to obtain compensated data under the above reference conditions. Fig. 3 shows that the catalyst activity is enhanced by increasing the reaction temperature, with the CO conversion approaching the equilibrium limit of the methanol synthesis reactions (1) and (2) at 538K. The corresponding Arrhenius plot gives apparent activation energy of 73.5kJ/mol, in reasonable agreement with reported values for similar catalysts and.

In Fig. 4, the effect on the CO conversion of varying the contact time is shown. As to be expected, the conversion of CO decreases as the syngas flow rate increases due to less contact time between catalyst particles and the gas phase. Contact times higher than 450ms g/ml are required to reach close to equilibrium conversion for the catalyst and conditions applied.

The selectivity to methanol obtained (defined as effluent molar flow rate of methanol to that of methanol and methane) varied between 98.7 and 100% depending on the reaction conditions. The methane selectivity was (correspondingly) always below 1.3%, and no other gaseous species were detected. Only trace concentrations of other oxygenates and higher alcohols were detected in the collected liquid in a few of the analyses and hence the liquid product was assumed to be consisting of methanol and water only in the mass balance calculations.

The high single-pass conversion achieved in IMPBRHE at isothermal conditions is a promising achievement, which could potentially provide high productivity. Small particles will definitely reduce internal mass transfer in methanol synthesis and hence increase the reaction rate. The possible contribution of external mass transfer limitations in IMPBRHE need also be considered, for which an experimental investigation is complicated by the flow conditions in the microchannels. Using an alternative approach of manipulating the gas phase diffusion, we found the IMPBRHE to be free of external mass transfer limitations under the conditions applied. The method, experimental details and results are presented elsewhere.

Fig. 5 presents the temperature profile measured on the reactor skin at different gas flow rates. The results indicate a gradient of 1–2K along the channel axis. This is regardless of the rate of the heat generation by the methanol synthesis at different conditions, i.e. high or low conversion. Temperature measurements were also performed by inserting a 0.5mm thermocouple in the missing row of pillars in the middle reaction slit. This turned out to be a challenging task with respect to controlling leaks at high pressure, and was therefore only applied in a few of the reaction experiments. The measurements showed, however, that the controlling factor of the slit temperatures is the inlet oil temperature. A reproducible correlation between the reaction slit temperature, skin temperatures and the inlet oil temperature was established provided that the system is well insulated. The maximum temperature difference between the inlet oil and the slit was around 3K. We assume that the reaction slit temperature is almost equal to the true reaction temperature, since it is a mixture of catalyst surface, gas and possibly wall temperature by contact of the thermocouple to all materials.

Table 2 shows values of the CO conversion obtained at different feed gas temperatures under otherwise equal conditions, including the reaction (skin) temperature. We find that varying the feed gas temperature has no significant effect on the conversion, which is a further indication of the good heat regulation capacity of the IMPBRHE. Although the feed gas enters the channel at a temperature of 20K lower than the reaction temperature, it rapidly heats up and reaches the channel temperature, because the channel temperature is governed by the inlet oil temperature.

Different types of resistance against heat transfer in the IMPBRHE may, however, exist inside the catalyst particles, in the gas phase, for the conduction through channel walls and finally in the heat exchange oil. For small catalyst particles (0.15–0.20mm), Graaf et al. showed that for methanol synthesis over Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst, a maximum temperature rise of only 0.1K is possible. This is similar to our case, where an even smaller average particle sizes was used. The pillar structures could also both improve the heat transfer in the gas phase by enhancing the mixing pattern and enhance the heat flux through the walls. To further investigate the heat removal capabilities, we also investigated the thermal characteristics of the IMPBRHE under methanol synthesis conditions through a modelling approach. A 2D pesudo-homogeous model for single reaction slit was developed using COMSOL Multiphysics. No velocity gradient is assumed to exist along the cross section, but axial and radial dispersion of heat and mass is included in the model. The kinetic expression derived by Vanden Bussche et al. for a commercial Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst was used for the reaction kinetic module. The mass and energy balance equations were integrated with the kinetics and the model was solved after applying initial and boundary conditions. Fig. 6 shows the simulation results generated by the model at contact time of 210ms g/ml and feed gas temperature of 493K. Except a temperature increase within a short region at the entrance (2–3mm) which is due to a somewhat lower feed gas temperature in the simulation, the slit remains isothermal and at a temperature equal to the wall temperature. This is in agreement with our observations in the lab which indicates near isothermal conditions. The level of productivity per unit volume of the slit obtained by the model, however, is higher than the experimental values due to lower activity of the catalyst used in the experiments.

The amount of heat generation in the methanol synthesis depends on the conversion level. Berty suggests a “Theoretical Adiabatic Temperature Rise” of around 170K under typical methanol synthesis operating conditions (corresponding to reaction rates of about 20mol/kg cat./h). The limited heat transfer capacity in industrial reactors dictates the process design towards application of larger contact times up to several seconds, while it should be possible to operate the reaction at less than 1s according to the literature kinetics. For a first order heterogeneous reaction (with respect to hydrogen in this study), the heat exchange time-scale is proportional to the square of characteristic channel dimension (∼d 2). This means that the heat exchange time should drop significantly by lowering the channel thickness. In addition, the isothermal operation may provide longer catalyst lifetime through preventing local hot spots that may accelerate sintering. Some catalyst deactivation, presumably not related to hot spot formation, was, however, observed in this study. The factors contributing to the deactivation have not yet been resolved and represent the objective of a separate investigation.

Superior heat removal capability of the IMPBRHE is revealed from both experimental and modelling results. Compared with co-current systems, the cross flow micro heat exchanger equipped with narrow fins gives the advantage of improved heat transfer over shorter flow lengths. Together with the high heat capacity of the heat transfer oil, a highly efficient heat removal system could be obtained. Moreover, the additional reactor surface area to volume provided by the pillar structure may further enhance heat transfer. The contact between catalyst particles and reactor wall is improved relative to a non-pillared packed slit, however less than that of a wall coated channel. Practically, the pillars act as heat sinks distributed across the slits to avoid heat accumulation, which may occur due to poor particle-wall contact in conventional fixed-bed reactors. All of these enhancements in key contributing factors in heat transfer processes suggest a thermally stable and isothermal reaction environment, which is easily controlled through the operating parameters of the heat transfer medium; i.e. oil flow rate and inlet temperature. In fact, the heat exchange capacity is probably larger than needed for the reaction volume of the IMPBRHE, and could potentially be downscaled or simplified under engineering. Before that, however, the productivity should be maximized through catalyst optimization.

Fig. 7 shows the measured values of the pressure drop against the superficial gas velocity obtained at room temperature and pressures of 1 (Fig. 7a) and 80bar (Fig. 7b). The measured values include the pressure drop caused by the two porous frits at the channels entrance and exit as well as over the packed catalyst particle bed. The measure values are compared to values calculated by the Ergun equation: (6) Δ P L = 150 ( 1 − ε ) 2 μ g u m ε 3 d p 2 + 1.75 ( 1 − ε ) ρ g u m 2 ε 3 d p where ɛ denotes the bed porosity, μ g the viscosity, u m the superficial gas velocity, L the channel length, d p the particle size, ρ g the density of the gas. Table 3 shows the parameters of the IMPBRHE and of the materials for the calculation of the pressure drop. For a completely laminar flow (Re<1 in this study), the second term of the Ergun equation is negligible.

At ambient pressure, the gas velocity is high and hence also the pressure drop. Good agreement exists between the measurements and the calculated values (Fig. 7a). When the pressure is increased to the operating pressure of methanol synthesis (80bar), the gas velocity is much lower and the resulting pressure drop also becomes much lower (Fig. 7b). The measured values at 80bar deviate from the calculated values, especially at very low velocities. The measured values are, however, almost outside of the accuracy limit of the measuring differential pressure transmitter. As the velocity increases, the measured and calculated values appear to converge.

Since the differential pressure transmitter could be applied at low temperatures only, measurements under reaction conditions were not possible. The methanol formation is associated with a reduction in the total number of moles, and hence the density of the gas and the viscosity decreases (mass is constant) whereas the velocity increases with the conversion along the reactor. The above values should therefore in principle be corrected to estimate the actual pressure drop. However, since the pressure drop is insignificant relative to the reaction pressure, we can ignore all these changes for practical application as well as modelling.

The issue of pressure drop is important whether a reactor is used as a tool for kinetic investigations or is part of a full-scale industrial operation. Although there are uncertainties in the estimation of pressure drop by the Ergun equation, such as porosity and particle diameter values as well as channel cross sectional area due to presence of the pillars, it appears that the equation gives a reasonable estimation of pressure drop in micro packed bed reactors. The more or less linear pressure drop against the gas velocity is furthermore an indication of laminar flow in the reaction channels under these conditions. Our study not only shows that the IMPBRHE is practically isobaric under relevant conditions, but also indicate that the pressure drop is not a major concern for scaling. Based on the results shown here, for a full-scale reactor module which is in the range of meters, the total pressure drop would not count more than a few percent of the operating pressure even at highest gas flow rates.

The hexagonally arranged pillar structure inside the slits splits the gas flow into a number of sub-streams. Each single reaction slit could be considered as up to five interconnected channels, in the following referred to as tunnels. Flow of gas over the pillars results in redistribution of flow and generates sinusoidal streamlines, which will enhance mixing of the individual tunnel streams. Flow passing the catalyst near the sidewalls of the slit will also be redirected into the core gas stream due to the pillars. The tunnel definition implicates a modified reactor characteristic length based on a tunnel hydraulic diameter.

Fig. 8a shows the velocity contours generated by FLUENT software for pillars with hexagonal cross section in an empty channel as a typical example. The flow velocity is low at the walls and around the pillars, while at the centre of tunnels, higher velocities are found. In Fig. 8b the results of a simulation with a porous body model in FLUENT is shown. In this case the porosity is 0.5 and spherical particles of 40μm are assumed. Whereas an empty pillar structure exhibits a velocity profile similar to a laminar straight channel, the packed pillar structure delivers a velocity profile which is almost uniform over the distance between the pillars. Fig. 8c shows the velocity magnitude collected at the half height in the packed slit along a line between the centres of two pillars in 60° angle to the main flow direction. The values are extracted from the cell planes which are touched by this line, so that the irregularities near the (pillar) wall is an artefact of the sampling. Nevertheless, Fig. 8c does indicate a more uniform velocity profile shown in Fig. 8b relative to an empty slit with pillars (Fig. 8a). We suppose that the same effect would be observed when comparing an empty and a packed single microchannel. Backmixing effects created by the particles themselves cannot be excluded, but from the simulations applying a porous body model we suppose that the Bodenstein numbers will increase due to the more uniform velocity profile.

The inlet and outlet tubing volume in IMPBRHE is considerably larger than the channels volume. In this context, large disturbances and undesired broadenings could be generated when applying traditional techniques for sampling of inlet and outlet streams and hence the results will be falsified. This was a barrier to experimental investigation of residence time distribution (RTD) in IMPBRHE. Among the parameters influencing RTD width in microchannels, the flow velocity (transition between laminar and turbulent) and diffusion coefficients may normally not be manipulated due to limitations in the operating window of chemical reactions. A possible solution to narrow the RTD would be to decrease the channel characteristic dimensions. Walter et al. showed how smaller channel cross sections generate narrower RTD curves. They also showed that a coated microchannel reactor can perform as a plug flow reactor with a narrow RTD curve when the diffusion coefficient is in the order of that of gases, i.e. 10−5 m2/s. Diffusion is the dominant mechanism for mass transport in the radial direction. In a micro packed bed reactor, however, the diffusion may be disturbed by particles. For methanol synthesis in the IMPBRHE, diffusion coefficients values are in the order of 10−6 m2/s and the necessary diffusion pathway would be longer due to the particles. The effect of axial diffusion could also remain important and mass transport was thus included in the modelling of methanol synthesis in the slit.

The RTD of the multichannel IMPBRHE could also be influenced by maldistribution of flow in individual slits caused by non-uniform packing. Since the catalyst is packed, application of techniques such as colour change, which could be used in coated wall microchannels as an indication of reaction intensity, is difficult. However, the even particle distribution observed in our glass slit in conjunction with the high reproducibility of conversion and selectivity levels upon applying different samples of the same catalyst batch, is another indication of even flow distribution between the slits. Further work on examination of cold flow distribution in a multi-slit IMPBRHE by hot wire anemometry technique using the same catalyst used in this study is planned. A theoretical comparison of RTD broadening in a conventional fixed-bed reactor and IMPBRHE has been performed by the authors elsewhere. Although we could not study the RTD in the IMPBRHE experimentally, it appears that the integrated pillar structure could improve the flow pattern to be plug flow-like. This will reduce the chance of disturbance of diffusion by the particles. The pillar structure also enhances mixing via redistribution and redirection of flow, ensuring good mass transfer properties even at very low Reynolds numbers.

Different characteristics of an Integrated Micro Packed Bed Reactor-Heat Exchanger (IMPBRHE) for compact production of methanol synthesis over Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst were investigated. Single-pass CO conversion levels achieved at relatively low contact times show that the productivity of such a reactor design could be promising. The reaction slit temperatures are controlled by the inlet temperature of the heat transfer oil. The measured as well as simulated temperature profiles along the individual channels in IMPBRHE indicate a fully isothermal behaviour under varying operating conditions. It was shown that the pressure drop over the micro packed bed system could be estimated by the Ergun equation. The linearity of the measured pressure drop against superficial gas velocities applied indicates a laminar flow regime. The magnitude of pressure drop relative to the total pressure is very low, so that even for a full-scale industrial module this is predicted as a less significant concern. The integrated pillar structures in the reaction slits improves fluid flow, mixing, heat and mass transfer properties of the reactor. The analysis of the IMPBRHE in this work shows that the methanol synthesis could potentially benefit from specific features of microstructured reactors. In addition, our study shows that by providing an isobaric and isothermal reaction media, the IMPBRHE is convenient tool for experimental investigation of catalytic reactions.
